title: Is work supposed to feel meaningful? We have trust issues.
summary: Season 2 finale mailbag episode: after roses and thorns on exercise routines, adjusting to single life and the emotional load of co-founding together, the sisters answer listener questions on repairing a friendship after lost trust, making friends in your late 20s and 30s, fulfillment in corporate versus entrepreneurship, and whether an MBA is worth it in a soft economy. Key takeaways: trust your gut, use best/worst/likely-case projections, treat friendship bids like the taxi-cab light, practice 'radical ownership', and view business school as a long-term play best timed to a weak job market.

ideas.idea: A consistent daily movement practice, even walking at 3.0 on a treadmill while calling a friend, changes how you feel and show up.
ideas.detail: Jean moved her body seven of seven days (gym classes, pickleball, tennis) and her Garmin shows a 90% body battery on six hours of sleep, which she attributes to sleeping deeper from exercise.

ideas.idea: There are different seasons for different things; a period of intense work after a life change is fine as long as you later rebalance socializing.
ideas.detail: Newly single after eight years and adjusting to a couples-oriented social circle, Jean has thrown herself into building Sisters with Cherie, working every day and weekend, and accepts this as a season rather than a permanent state.

ideas.idea: Putting things on the calendar to look forward to, big and small, makes the grind of building a company easier.
ideas.detail: Cherie plans a May trip to Japan, a board game night with GSB friends and a symphony outing with a new friend; having outlets and breaks scheduled is a psychological tool for her.

ideas.idea: Co-founders are valuable because you can spiral at different times and talk each other out of it; being a solo founder means being strong for yourself always.
ideas.detail: Cherie feels she must stay overly positive when an episode underperforms so as not to kill momentum; she recalls a co-founder breakup at her earlier startup Outdoor Pass that left her effectively solo. The sisters debate a friend's claim that three co-founders is the sweet spot for tie-breaks, with Jean pushing back that one person can end up ganged up on.

ideas.idea: If you have lost trust in a friend, it is for a good reason, and rebuilding requires both parties giving 100%, not 50/50.
ideas.detail: Jean's instinct is to write off a friendship once trust is gone; Cherie believes repair is possible with time, work and tears, but the bigger red flag is the other person avoiding the conversation and not being equally invested.

ideas.idea: Before deciding whether to reconcile, run a thought exercise of the best case, worst case and most likely scenario to feel out the range of outcomes.
ideas.detail: Jean describes this as a derivation of cognitive behavioral therapy: a safe 'dry run of the feelings' done alone that often produces a gut answer about whether the friendship has run its course.

ideas.idea: Ask whether a breach of trust was circumstantial or endemic to the person's personality, because that predicts whether it will happen again.
ideas.detail: A one-time situational lapse can be repaired; a trait the person refuses or cannot reasonably be expected to change is a different matter.

ideas.idea: Trust your gut; it is faster than cognitive understanding and ignoring it has always been to your peril.
ideas.detail: Jean notes that leaving an interaction with a bubbly, seemingly nice person yet feeling uncomfortable inside is your gut flagging caution, and the earlier you learn to trust it the better.

ideas.idea: To make friends in your late 20s and 30s, openly tell existing friends the kind of people you want to meet; people genuinely want to connect you.
ideas.detail: Jean has connected friends who are new or expecting moms with each other after they voiced that need; new life stages, interests or careers call for proactively seeking like-minded people.

ideas.idea: Seek out spaces built around shared experiences or activities, such as business school, a pottery class or a networking event, to cultivate friendships.
ideas.detail: Cherie found a two-year MBA program with peers seeking the same experience extremely rich for friendships; activity-based settings produce fruitful conversations.

ideas.idea: The taxi-cab theory applies to friendship: an unreturned bid usually means the other person's light is off, not that it's personal.
ideas.detail: Some people lack bandwidth for new relationships at a given time, so you have to put out enough bids to find someone in the same open mindset and not be discouraged by non-reciprocation.

ideas.idea: Corporate fulfillment comes from scale of influence, while entrepreneurial fulfillment comes from percentage of ownership over the outcome.
ideas.detail: Jean led M&A worth hundreds of millions of dollars in corporate; at Sisters each sister is by definition 50% of the company's impact, i.e. more ownership of a smaller pie versus less ownership of a much larger one.

ideas.idea: Politicking and layers of abstraction drain builders in corporate roles; know whether you are a builder or a manager archetype.
ideas.detail: Cherie, a computer scientist who identifies as a builder, was frustrated by PRDs, strategy docs, design reviews and approvals at big tech; now the sisters ship faster because they trust each other and 90% of the time approve each other's work.

ideas.idea: Buyer beware: in entrepreneurship you have massive control but you are also the sole point of failure, with no one to blame.
ideas.detail: In corporate you can say a decision wasn't approved by the CFO or a designer ignored feedback; as founders every outcome is felt fully and belongs to you.

ideas.idea: Radical ownership, the mindset that if you see a problem it is yours to figure out, is rare in big tech and a must-have when hiring.
ideas.detail: Jean refuses to work with people who pass the buck; Zynga's motto 'be your own CEO' embodied this, and she saw it in the best PMs and engineers but also many who said 'not my problem'. Cherie references Kim Scott's Radical Candor by analogy.

ideas.idea: If you want an environment where you can sometimes say 'not my problem', corporate life will be more fulfilling; you need to be set up for the phase of life where entrepreneurship can succeed.
ideas.detail: The sisters stress that fulfillment is personal and that different life phases suit different environments.

ideas.idea: At a lean startup, candidates who ask about work-life balance usually don't work out, according to a founder friend.
ideas.detail: A Columbia-in-Tech co-founder said he has worked 100-hour weeks and weekends for three years; hires who asked about balance tended to underperform within three months. Jean doesn't find this crazy since Goldman Sachs, Zynga and Snap all expected working past midnight to 2-3 AM.

ideas.idea: Business school is a long-term play whose payoff comes from people and experiences over the fullness of time, not just the first job out.
ideas.detail: Cherie is about to collaborate with an MBA classmate on Sisters merchandise, a connection she never anticipated; in the soft 2024-2025 hiring market fewer grads get finance, tech and consulting jobs and more turn to entrepreneurship.

ideas.idea: The best time to attend business school is when the economy is soft, because the opportunity cost of being off the job market for two years is lowest.
ideas.detail: Jean contrasts this with the 2020-2021 hiring frenzy when you wanted to be on the market; being in school during a downturn means building skills to rejoin at a higher level rather than 'convalescing'. She qualifies that some people attend for a discrete short-term pivot.

ideas.idea: Intense finance work cultures that push analysts into health and mental-health problems deserve open discussion.
ideas.detail: The sisters flag this as a future episode topic, noting Jean has 'war stories' from coworkers and friends.
